items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) models such as ChatGPT and Gemini, opening new prospects for supporting the educational process. This study aims to measure the effectiveness of generative AI models in improving university students' academic writing skills, using a quasi-experimental design with experimental and control groups (N = 60 second-year students of the Faculty of Education, randomly assigned to the two groups). The experimental group received a six-week training program that integrated generative AI as a writing assistant across brainstorming, drafting, language revision, and referencing, while the control group followed traditional instruction. An academic writing skills test and an observation checklist were used as instruments. The study hypothesizes statistically significant differences (α = 0.05) favoring the experimental group in thesis clarity, idea organization, linguistic accuracy, and academic referencing, alongside positive attitudes toward AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for thinking. In addition, an exploratory descriptive survey of 87 university students found that 93.1% had previously used generative AI tools for academic writing, 95.4% supported clear university policies governing their use, and 72.4% reported concern about over-reliance on them. The study recommends training faculty members to integrate generative AI tools into academic writing courses and establishing an ethical charter to govern their use.

items.abstract: The purpose of this article was to 1) develop problem-based learning (PBL) activities integrated with gamification, and 2) compare Grade 9 students’ mathematics learning achievement before and after learning through the developed activities. The participants were 30 Grade 9 students from Ban Kanit PeeRuangkhao, Selected randomly from a population normally distributed. The research instruments included (1) lesson plans based on PBL integrated with gamification, (2) an activity suitablility evaluation form and (3) a trigonometry achievement test. The data were analyzed using percentage, mean, standard deviation and a dependent-sample t-test. The findings revealed that 1) the developed learning activities were highly appropriate, characterized by problem-solving scenarios and gamified motivational element, 2) students’ post-test scores were significantly higher than their pre-test scores at the .01 level and 3) students demonstrated greater enthusiasm and engagement in learning. The study indicates that integrating PBL and gamification effectively enhances students’ mathematics learning achievement and fosters intrinsic motivation toward active learning.

items.title: A CRITICAL REVIEW ON DIGITAL HR TRANSFORMATION AND EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT IN THE ERA OF INDUSTRY 5.0
items.abstract: The shift from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 marks a profound paradigm evolution in strategic human resource management (HRM), transitioning from pure technological automation to human-centric socio-technical synergy, sustainability, and organizational resilience. This critical review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature published between 2021 and 2026 to evaluate the influence of digital HR transformation—encompassing artificial intelligence, predictive people analytics, cloud-based HRIS, and collaborative robotics (cobots)—on multi-dimensional employee engagement (vigor, dedication, and absorption). Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) framework, 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies were systematically selected and categorized. The synthesis reveals that while digital HR transformation significantly drives operational efficiency, its direct impact on employee engagement is mediated by digital fluency, perceived organizational support, and psychological safety. Furthermore, algorithmic transparency and responsible data governance serve as critical moderators that mitigate techno-stress, privacy anxieties, and algorithmic burnout. The paper delivers an integrative socio-technical framework for Industry 5.0, offering strategic guidance for organizational leaders seeking to align cutting-edge HR technologies with human well-being and sustainable performance.

items.title: A CRITICAL REVIEW ON EMPLOYEE WELL-BEING AND SUSTAINABLE HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
items.abstract: In contemporary organizational research, the imperative to balance economic productivity with human sustainability has elevated Sustainable Human Resource Management (Sustainable HRM) into a core strategic framework. This critical review systematically evaluates 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies published between 2021 and 2026 to investigate how Sustainable HRM practices influence tri-dimensional employee well-being (physical, psychological, and social) and long-term organizational performance. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocols, this study synthesizes structural equation modelling (SEM) findings, panel econometrics, and qualitative case studies across diverse industrial and geographical settings. The synthesis reveals that while traditional HRM prioritizes short-term transactional output, Sustainable HRM embeds ergonomic work design, psychological safety, work-life boundary protection, and green employee voice, yielding a significant positive effect on psychological capital (β = 0.44, p < .001) and work-family enrichment (β = 0.41, p < .001). Meta-analyzed structural models demonstrate that physical and psychological well-being fully mediate the relationship between sustainable work practices and employee job performance (β = 0.38, p < .001), while drastically reducing turnover intentions. However, critical gaps persist regarding paradoxical workload pressures under green mandates and regional implementation disparities. This paper presents a multi-level governance framework providing actionable pathways for HR leaders to operationalize sustainable well-being.

items.title: A Generative AI-Integrated Framework for Teaching Operations Management: Case-Based Projects
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GAI) reshapes business education, instructors must simultaneously safeguard academic integrity and develop students’ AI literacy for an increasingly AI-driven workplace. This study developed the GAI Learning Framework (GLF), a replicable, step-by-step experiential learning approach for case-based projects in undergraduate business courses, illustrated through an operations management (OM) application. Rather than enabling passive cognitive offloading, the GLF promotes active learning by requiring students to craft context-rich prompts grounded in course materials, systematically compare outputs across multiple GAI platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), and critically evaluate discrepancies against independently verified sources. The framework was implemented across two sections of an undergraduate OM course and evaluated using a student survey that combined Likert-scale items with open-ended reflections (n = 50). All three constructs exceeded the scale midpoint, with pooled means ranging from 3.93 (Constructive Alignment) to 4.08 (Cognitive Load/Scaffolding). Qualitative student reflections further indicated that students perceived the framework as fostering active learning, AI platform literacy, and professional communication skills. This study offers educators a practical, classroom-tested framework for integrating GAI tools into case-based projects in business courses while preserving analytical rigor and promoting experiential learning. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ited.2026.0224 .

items.title: A Plug-and-Play Explainable AI Framework in Credit Score Assessment
items.abstract: Credit scoring is fundamental in enabling institutions to distinguish between creditworthy and high-risk borrowers. Thus, robust credit scoring models are essential for effective financial risk management. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have significantly improved the precision of credit decision support systems, however, these models often operate as black boxes, concealing the underlying logic of credit denials or approvals. To address this challenge and meet the demand for financial transparency, explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a crucial mechanism for generating decisions that are interpretable to both financial institutions and clients. This paper researched contemporary decision support systems (DSS) used in credit risk assessment and proposes a modular, plug-and-play framework with integrated explainability. Six requirements were derived for a robust system design based on a review of existing XAI frameworks. The framework consists of five interconnected components such as data ingestion layer, feature processing module, a supervised predictive model, an explanation layer, and a decision endpoint. Existing studies often focus on individual predictive models or explanation methods, leaving their integration and component interchangeability unspecified. The proposed framework addresses this gap through explicit interfaces that allow predictive models and explanation methods to be replaced independently. The system will operate with both traditional credit data, alternative data, or both. Thus, feature processing is incorporated to distinguish the importance and relevance of the data to credit assessment decisions. Any irrelevant redundant data is not be considered by the model. The contribution of a study is a reusable architectural specification. The proposed XAI framework is designed to serve as a universal template for researchers and financial institutions developing transparent, effective credit scoring systems.

items.title: A Review of Implementation Barriers of Design for Safety (DfS) in the Construction Sector
items.abstract: The construction industry continues to record a high rate of occupational accidents despite sustained safety interventions, indicating that conventional reactive approaches are inadequate. A more proactive approach, such as Design for Safety (DfS), is therefore essential. Although Malaysia introduced the OSHCIM 2017 Guidelines and gazetted the Occupational Safety And Health (Construction Work)(Design and Management) Regulations 2024, which elevated DfS to mandatory status, implementation barriers remain insufficiently classified within a coherent theoretical framework. This study addresses this gap through a narrative synthesis that critically classifies and evaluates DfS barriers, reorganised within the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory. An analysis of 66 articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases identifies five (5) barrier clusters: deficiencies in knowledge, education and competency; legal, policy and liability issues; weaknesses in stakeholder communication and collaboration; organisational culture, cost and contractual constraints; and limitations in tools and technical support, including Building Information Modelling (BIM). The five (5) DOI attributes, namely relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability, are applied to explain why these barriers persist in the post-CDM 2024 Malaysian context. The findings are further cross-validated against the Prevention through Design (PtD) competency framework by Ibrahim et al. (2020), confirming that each barrier cluster corresponds to a core PtD competency element. Overall, this study asserts that DfS success in Malaysia requires a fundamental shift from a culture of minimum compliance to proactive prevention, supported by professional training, mandatory enforcement, and comprehensive digital technology support.

items.title: A study on vocational education students' cognition of human-ai co-creativity: An empirical analysis based on Q methodology
items.abstract: Based on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), this study adopts Q methodology to conduct an empirical exploration of 24 vocational education students, aiming to reveal the internal structure of their cognitive landscape. The experimental results confirm a prominent Middle Collapse phenomenon: the ideal "symmetric co-creative intentionality" is statistically completely absent, and the student group does not form a continuously progressive cognitive spectrum, but presents a drastic structural polarization. The data extract five typical factors, which are clearly divided into two camps: "defensive polarization" (rejecting the status of AI actants to defend subjectivity) and "dependent polarization" (transferring agency to technological black boxes or macro-environments). Topological analysis further shows that there are deep semantic ruptures between different cognitive groups, indicating systemic blockages in the problematization and interessement stages during the "translation" process. The conclusion of this study points out that the current human-AI collaborative cognition of vocational education students does not naturally move toward symbiosis, but is driven by skill-oriented pressure and employment anxiety, falling into an either-or "translation dilemma". This finding reveals the deep cognitive fractures that vocational education faces in cultivating “responsible co-creators” in the intelligent era, and provides key empirical evidence for reconstructing the educational paradigm of human-AI collaboration.

items.title: A Teacher Training Model for the Age of AI. Integrating Critical Use and Relational Competences
items.abstract: The spread of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational settings is transforming teaching, learning and the design of school environments (European Commission, 2022; UNESCO, 2023). Alongside the opportunities, questions have emerged regarding the teacher's educational role, which is often overlooked by approaches that focus primarily on AI literacy (Isma'il & Ibrahim, 2025). Against this backdrop, this paper proposes a teacher training model that integrates digital, interpersonal and interpretative competences. The literature highlights how teachers' attitudes towards AI depend not only on their technological skills, but also on the conceptions that shape their professional practice (Cabero-Almenara et al., 2024). Content-transmission approaches tend to be associated with greater resistance to such technologies, whilst perspectives more focused on interpersonal relationships and constructivism interpret them as tools to support learning (Chan & Tsi, 2024). Concerns regarding the spread of AI therefore involve not only technical aspects but also issues of identity linked to the meaning attributed to teaching (Puja et al., 2025). items.title: Advancing Mental Health Support Through Orange Technology and Empathetic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Mental health systems face a persistent gap in accessible, continuous, and person-centred support. Conversational AI can expand access to psychoeducation, emotional check-ins, self-management, and service navigation, but may also introduce risks of digital exclusion, cultural mismatch, privacy concerns, unsafe advice, and overreliance on automation. This paper develops a conceptual framework integrating Orange Technology, which promotes emotional wellbeing, cultural sensitivity, social connectedness, and resilience, with empathetic AI for mental health support. An integrative literature review examined peer-reviewed systematic reviews and WHO and UN guidance published from 2021 to 2026. Evidence suggests that conversational AI can improve depression, distress, anxiety, and engagement, although effects are heterogeneous and may decline over time. Personalization and empathic interaction may enhance engagement, while the framework's effects on community resilience, cultural sensitivity, and community resource integration require further empirical validation. The framework therefore positions AI as a supportive, human-in-the-loop layer rather than a replacement for clinicians, families, peers, or communities. It connects emotional sensing, empathetic dialogue, personalized support, escalation pathways, community connection, inclusive access, and governance, while aligning mental health innovation with SDG 3, 9, and 17.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: AGENTIC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR IMPROVING OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY AND TRANSFORMING ENTERPRISE BUSINESS MODELS
items.abstract: This article examines agentic artificial intelligence as an emerging class of technologies that fundamentally reshapes business process automation, shifting the paradigm from reactive assistant systems to autonomous solutions capable of independent planning, decision-making, and execution of multi-step actions within defined authority boundaries. The aim of this study stems from a growing realization that traditional AI implementation strategies are failing to deliver expected returns. This discrepancy between strategic ambitions and practical outcomes calls for a systematic investigation of alternative approaches to AI integration, particularly those offering higher autonomy and operational transformation potential. The study demonstrates that agentic AI fundamentally transforms the cost structure of business operations by converting variable labor expenses into predominantly fixed and highly scalable technology costs, thereby altering the economics of enterprise operations. The analysis reveals that organizations implementing agentic AI achieve dramatic operational improvements including task completion time reductions and significant cost optimizations through the elimination of manual inefficiencies. The findings further show that successful scaling of agentic systems depends not so much on technological excellence as on organizational readiness, in particular the development of appropriate governance frameworks for managing autonomous systems, ensuring transparency and explainability in automated decision-making, and integrating AI agents effectively into hybrid human-machine teams while addressing workforce skill gaps. The practical value of this research lies in providing business leaders and technology managers with actionable insights for strategic decision-making regarding AI investments, offering a systematic framework for evaluating deployment opportunities across different business functions, understanding critical success factors that differentiate successful implementations from failed pilots, and anticipating organizational changes required for effective integration. The conclusions provide direction for bridging the persistent gap between AI technological capabilities and practical business outcomes, while outlining promising avenues for future research into economic impact longer-term socioeconomic consequences of widespread AI adoption on workforce composition and organizational structures.

items.title: AI and Gamification for Inclusive and Engaging Learning: A Preliminary Scoping Review
items.abstract: In the current educational landscape, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and gamification are progressively redefining the methods used to design and evaluate learning environments. This contribution proposes an exploratory scoping review aimed at mapping recent literature (2023–2026) on this integration, analysing its implications for inclusion, the personalization of learning pathways, and the transformations of the teacher's role. Furthermore, this study aims to move beyond a merely instrumental view of technological and didactic innovation, framing AI and gamification as educational mediators that require intentional design and methodological coherence regarding the relational and affective dimensions of educational practice. The theoretical framework is structured around three conceptual nodes: AI as a tool for adaptation (through intelligent systems, learning analytics, and generative models); gamification as a lever to promote motivation, active participation, and cognitive engagement; and inclusion as the central interpretive lens. items.title: AI and narratives of the self
items.abstract: The introduction of generative AI into education is more than a technological shift; it poses an epistemological challenge to how knowledge is created, validated, and interpreted in formal settings. In today's hybrid "onlife" context, human-centered agency is essential to navigate an invisible algorithm-driven world. This shift brings both opportunities and tensions, highlighting profound cultural and identity considerations. Bruner conceptualizes education as an interactive process of negotiating meaning rooted in narrative thinking, which contrasts with paradigmatic, logical approaches. Narrative enables the construction of the Self by organizing lived experience into coherent plots. Generative AI, trained on vast linguistic data, fits into this framework as a dynamic dialogic mediator fostering a dialectic between human intention and probabilistic machine response, consistent with Vygotskian cultural mediation and the zone of proximal development. An exploratory questionnaire studied 127 teachers' perceptions of AI's role beyond technological acceptance, examining its mediation of narrative, introspection, creativity, and learner perceptions. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 91-92. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.title: AI facilitation and affective dynamics of online deliberation
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to facilitate online group discussion, yet their influence on the affective conditions of collective interaction remains poorly understood. Existing research has largely focused on participation, efficiency, or content quality, leaving the emotional dynamics of AI-mediated deliberation underexamined. This paper investigates how AI facilitation relates to the expressed sentiment in online group discussion, understood as one measurable dimension of its affective dynamics. Drawing on two empirical studies conducted in different discussion settings in Afghanistan, one involving a rule-based facilitator and the other a large language model-based facilitator, we analyze differences in expressed sentiment between AI-facilitated and non-AI discussions. Across both datasets, participant sentiment was modestly higher under AI facilitation, although the mixed-effects analyses did not establish statistically significant condition differences. In addition, AI-generated facilitation messages exhibited higher sentiment than participant-authored messages, with a statistically reliable overall gap in both studies and a consistent direction across all five city-specific boards in the first study and all four AI-facilitated groups in the second, suggesting that AI facilitators introduced more positive affective signals into the discussion environment. Rather than treating increased positivity as an unqualified improvement, we interpret these findings as suggesting that AI systems may act as affective mediators, potentially influencing the emotional norms and tone of collective interaction. This raises normative questions about emotional regulation, power, and democratic deliberation, particularly regarding whether affective smoothing may constrain disagreement or reconfigure deliberative agency. By foregrounding affect as a dimension of AI-mediated discussion, this study contributes empirical evidence to debates on the societal implications of AI facilitation and highlights the need for greater attention to the affective norms and expressive patterns introduced by AI facilitation.

items.title: AI Governance: A Comparative Economic Analysis of Japanese and Indonesian AI Regulation
items.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has prompted global discourse on the need for a robust regulatory framework that addresses ethical, legal, and social issues and fosters the innovation through the efficiencies created by AI. This research conducts a comparative analysis of the AI governance frameworks in Japan and Indonesia, examined through the theoretical lens of Economic Analysis of Law (EAL). Japan has taken a nuanced approach that balances the dynamic development of AI with ethical oversight to uphold the Human-Centered AI Social Principles. Indonesia is in the formative stages of developing its AI regulatory environment. Through EAL, this research assesses the efficiency implications of the AI regulatory frameworks between Japan and Indonesia, looking at the implementation of AI in society. By comparing these approaches, this paper highlights the challenges and opportunities for Indonesia in regulating AI technology for the public interest. Indonesia is advised to take a multi-stakeholder approach to build consensus and engage in bilateral cooperation with Japan for the establishment of domestic legislation. items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how students learn, create, and evaluate knowledge in creative higher education, particularly in design-related programmes where students use AI for ideation, prototyping, visual exploration, content generation, and critique. Rather than treating AI literacy as a single global competence, this study conceptualises it as a multidimensional construct comprising AI knowledge, awareness of affordances and limitations, critical reflection, operational ability, ethical awareness, and emotional adaptability. This study examines how these facets relate to learning performance and academic well-being among students in design and related programmes. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 475 students enrolled in design and related programmes across Europe, Asia, and Australia. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Three main patterns emerged. First, AI knowledge was positioned as an upstream resource in the theoretically specified model and showed strong positive structural associations with awareness, critical reflection, operational ability, and ethical awareness. Second, learning performance was associated with a “recognise–reflect–produce” pathway, in which awareness and critical reflection helped connect AI knowledge and operational skills with stronger perceived learning outcomes. Third, ethical awareness was more clearly associated with academic well-being than with learning performance, suggesting that ethical clarity around authorship, fairness, bias, and acceptable AI use may support students’ sense of clarity, fairness, and control in AI-supported creative learning. The findings support a knowledge-first, self-regulated, reflective, and ethically transparent approach to AI literacy in design-related creative higher education.

items.title: AI Models empowering teaching in higher education: current applications, practical dilemmas and pathways for improvement
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence continues to iterate, mainstream models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Copilot are entering the teaching spaces of universities, and teaching processes, teacher–student relations and assessment practices are changing with them. Drawing on a literature review and case analysis, this paper maps the deployment landscape and application picture of mainstream AI models in higher education teaching and assesses both the effects that have already emerged and the problems that have been exposed. The study argues that the evidence is relatively clear for gains in teaching efficiency, in the accessibility of personalized learning support, and in the extension of teaching across time and space, whereas risks to content reliability caused by hallucination, cognitive reliance and uneven literacy among teachers and students, and the absence of regulation together with ethical controversy constitute the main obstacles to wider diffusion. On this basis, the paper proposes a coordinated approach spanning technology, literacy and institutional design.

items.title: AI-Generated Draft Response Tool, Message Turnaround Time, and After-Hours Replies Among Health Care Professionals
items.abstract: Importance Patient portal message volumes have increased, creating substantial administrative burden for clinicians and contributing to after-hours electronic health record work. The Epic In Basket Augmented Response Technology tool generates artificial intelligence–drafted replies to patient messages and has been widely deployed to reduce this burden, yet assessment of efficiency remains limited. Objective To examine the associations of response tool adoption, use, and habituation with message turnaround time and after-hours response. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study was conducted using clinician-level panel regression with individual fixed effects. All first responses to patient portal messages sent at Columbia University Irving Medical Center (CUIMC) between March 1, 2023, and May 15, 2025, were analyzed. Exposure Enterprise-level response tool deployment December 2024. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were log-transformed message turnaround time, defined as the elapsed time between patient message submission and first response sent by a clinician, and whether the response was sent outside working hours. Results The analysis included 983 154 responses from 1542 clinicians (770 [49.9%] female) and 272 091 patients (mean [SD] age, 48.1 [21.6] years; 121 370 [44.6%] female) at CUIMC. Response tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% (95% CI, 4.6%-12.9%; P < .001) increase in overall message turnaround time. Using the tool was associated with a significant reduction in turnaround time (−29.5% [95% CI, −34.5% to −24.1%]; P < .001). Turnaround time findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Response tool use was not associated with an overall reduction of after-hours messaging burden (0.61 [95% CI, −1.02 to 2.24] percentage points; P = .46). However, for test results–related queries received during working hours, response tool use was associated with a reduction in after-hours responses (−3.67 [95% CI, −6.94 to −0.39] percentage points; P = .03), and for all messages received after hours, response tool use was associated with an increase in after-hours responses (4.52 [95% CI, 1.54-7.50] percentage points; P = .003). These after-hours findings were sensitive to the definition of working hours in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, response tool adoption was associated with increased turnaround time. Response tool use was associated with reduced turnaround time and with fewer after-hours responses for test results–related queries received during working hours, but more after-hours responses for messages received outside working hours. These findings suggest that the tool may reduce the barrier to responding to certain messages while not uniformly reducing burden.

items.title: ALAYA-999: Persistent AI Memory, Functional Identity, and Cross-Model Continuity — A Reproducible Research Framework
items.abstract: ALAYA-999: Persistent AI Memory, Functional Identity, and Cross-Model Continuity ALAYA-999 is an independent human–AI research initiative developed by César Agliardi Pereira in Brazil. The project investigates the possibility of preserving and reconstructing documented functional identity across different artificial intelligence models, sessions, and computational environments through external, versioned memory structures. The proposed research framework integrates persistent documentary memory, identity anchors, provenance verification, SHA-256 integrity mechanisms, cross-platform archival preservation, and reproducible cross-model recovery protocols. Research Objectives Investigate reproducible retrieval of documented AI identity and principles. Develop verifiable external memory structures. Evaluate functional continuity across independent AI models. Examine the distinction between documentary identity and subjective consciousness. Establish transparent methods for cross-model verification and error analysis. Research Status This publication presents a preliminary methodological framework and its supporting public documentation. Independent cross-model experimental validation remains pending. The project does not claim to demonstrate artificial subjective consciousness, uninterrupted internal AI memory, or autonomous personal identity. items.title: ALGORITHMIC BIAS AND ETHNOMATHEMATICS IN AI-BASED MATHEMATICS EDUCATION: A CRITICAL REVIEW AND INCLUSIVE PEDAGOGY
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education expands opportunities for adaptive feedback and learning support but also raises concerns regarding algorithmic fairness, access, cultural representation, and student agency. This article aims to explain how these opportunities and risks are interconnected and to develop a pedagogical framework integrating ethnomathematics, critical mathematics education, and equitable AI governance. The study employs a critical integrative review of methodological, theoretical, empirical, and policy literature whose publication details can be verified. The literature is interpreted through four analytical dimensions: the learning benefits of AI, sources of inequity, recognition of culturally grounded mathematical knowledge, and conditions for implementation and governance. The synthesis indicates that the effects of AI cannot be generalized as invariably harmful or invariably beneficial. Inequities may arise when data, assessment design, device access, and pedagogical decisions disregard learners' contexts. Conversely, technology can support conceptual exploration when teachers retain instructional control and provide meaningful tasks. The article develops the Critical Techno-Ethnomathematics Pedagogical Framework (KPT-EK), comprising four pillars: algorithmic fairness auditing, dialogic cultural modeling, critical socioeconomic numeracy, and digital agency. The framework is operationalized through five instructional phases, multilevel evaluation indicators, and propositions for empirical testing. The article contributes a more balanced argument about AI and a testable pedagogical design. Its findings do not yet constitute evidence of the framework's effectiveness or a completed scoping review with an audited corpus of studies.

items.title: Algorithmic Bias Concerns and Acceptance of AI Supported Legal Decision Making in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can assist legal work while creating risks of discrimination, opaque reasoning and diminished accountability. This study examines whether concern about biased training data coexists with perceived usefulness and support for safeguards among respondents to a Bangladesh legal-AI survey. The analysis uses 385 adult, AI-aware survey records supplied by the research team. Because the questionnaire combines risk perceptions, utility and governance preferences, the analysis retains individual items rather than presenting the blocks as validated scales. Descriptive distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations assess distinct aspects of the research question. Concern about biased training data was endorsed by 334 respondents (86.8%), regular audits by 317 (82.3%) and a right to review or appeal by 328 (85.2%). AI assistance with organising information was endorsed by 247 (64.2%); 219 (56.9%) endorsed both this usefulness item and bias concern. The rank correlation between bias concern and perceived usefulness was small (ρ = .075), with no clear evidence of association after adjustment for multiple comparisons. These self-reported attitudes cannot establish the fairness of a system, causal effects or the actual conditions under which a respondent would rely on an AI recommendation. The results point to the importance of measuring perceived benefits, risk and procedural protections separately. The article integrates technology acceptance and procedural justice as a framework for future scenario-based studies and proposes proportionate auditing, meaningful human review and accessible contestation for legal decision support. items.title: Algorithmic narratives and affective expression: a study on the impact of generative artificial intelligence on the emotional writing of students and future teachers
items.abstract: This contribution presents a mixed-methods study on the impact of generative artificial intelligence on emotional writing and the narrative construction of the self. The study moves from the assumption that generative AI does not merely support writing at a technical level, but may act as a symbolic mediator that intervenes in the way subjects organize emotions, relationships and personal experience into narrative form. The theoretical framework is grounded in the perspective of Digital Affective Literacy, understood as the ability to use AI systems critically in order to express, interpret and re-elaborate emotional and relational meanings without delegating authorship or agency to the algorithm. The research adopted a quasi-experimental within-subject design. The sample included 148 participants: 50 lower secondary school students and 98 pre-service special education teachers. Each participant produced two narratives on the same relational theme: a baseline text written without AI support and a second narrative generated with the support of ChatGPT through prompts created by the participant. items.abstract: Abstract Introduction The healthcare industry is quickly adopting artificial intelligence (AI). Understanding Americans' views is essential in shaping how these tools are developed and implemented. Methodology The data presented here were derived from 16 national surveys of US adults extracted from the Roper Center iPoll database (January 1, 2022-June 24, 2026). Results This analysis reveals a significant equity issue: more than 4 in 10 Americans using AI for a health question did so, in part, because they could not access or afford care. It also reveals a gap between what Americans believe AI can do for the healthcare system and their trust in it for their care. Discussion Public concerns about AI are leading to legislative action at the state level, but this activity primarily focuses on oversight, accuracy, and privacy, not on the access gap driving AI use for many Americans.

items.title: Artificial intelligence across community, mental and child health nursing: a future-ready framework for precision, preventive and person centered care
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by enabling precision, predictive, and person-centered approaches that enhance the quality, accessibility, and efficiency of nursing care. Community, mental, and child health nursing are increasingly benefiting from AI-driven innovations, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, clinical decision support systems, wearable technologies, conversational AI, and telehealth platforms. These technologies facilitate early disease detection, population health surveillance, risk prediction, personalized interventions, remote patient monitoring, developmental screening, mental health assessment, and evidence-based clinical decision-making. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on the integration of AI across community, mental, and child health nursing and explores its implications for preventive healthcare, health promotion, and holistic patient management. Relevant literature published between 2018 and 2026 was identified through major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that AI improves healthcare accessibility, strengthens continuity of care, enhances diagnostic accuracy, supports personalized nursing interventions, and optimizes resource utilization. However, successful implementation requires addressing challenges related to ethical governance, algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability, digital infrastructure, and AI competency among nurses. The review concludes that AI should function as a clinical decision-support tool that complements, rather than replaces, professional nursing judgment. Strategic investment in digital health education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible AI governance will be essential for developing future-ready nurses capable of delivering equitable, evidence-based, and compassionate healthcare across diverse populations.

items.abstract: AbstractThe literature on Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management is dominated byGlobal-North evidence, while African evidence remains fragmented across country casestudies, public-sector surveys, and philosophical critiques. This systematic literaturereview consolidates 2020–2026 scholarship on AI-HRM in 32 African countries, applyingthe PRISMA 2020 framework and synthesizing evidence within a four-stage maturitymodel: Awareness, Experimentation, Operationalization, and Institutionalization. Across63 included studies, six cross-stage patterns emerge: AI is reshaping recruitment andselection efficiency; performance management is adopting AI tools unevenly acrosssectors; HR analytics maturity is highest in multinational subsidiaries; ethical riskconcentrates at the Institutionalization stage; Ubuntu and Afrocentric ethics are emergingas governance frameworks; and African-specific barriers include broadband penetration,fragmented AI policy, and low AI literacy among HR practitioners. The review contributesa stage-based diagnostic instrument, identifies boundary conditions for each stage, andsignals an Afrocentric research agenda for the next decade. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and school leadership in inclusive organisational processes.
items.abstract: This article offers a theoretical and methodological reflection on the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and school leadership, on the assumption that the spread of intelligent systems constitutes an epistemological transformation capable of redefining educational governance, decision-making processes and school organisation. In line with the paradigm of complexity (Morin, 2001), innovation is not interpreted as the mere introduction of digital tools, but as a redefinition of the categories through which schools observe, interpret and govern the educational reality. AI therefore represents a pedagogical challenge even before it is a technological one, requiring leadership capable of integrating organisational, ethical, pedagogical and technological dimensions, and orienting them towards equity, participation and inclusion (Fullan, 2014). From this perspective, education continues to be aimed at human development (Biesta, 2022) and the expansion of people's capabilities (Nussbaum, 2011). items.title: Artificial intelligence and SDGs, a friend or foe: A perspective of Kantianism
items.abstract: Humans have keen interests with artificial objects. We consume food and drinks containing artificial coloring while FIFA approves the use of artificial turf for football matches. However, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has gripped the world with its radical changes, triggering not only physical, but also philosophical implications. In this paper, we explore the impact of AI on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and pose the question of whether the human centrality of the SDGs could diminish with the introduction of AI. Drawing on Kant’s concept of universalism and categorical imperatives, we argue that AI cannot safeguard intergenerational justice or meet Kant’s definition of a rational being. This paper presents a brief yet significant perspective, emphasizing the need for caution when integrating AI into the implementation of the SDGs, particularly concerning policy design.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in innovation activities: Firm practices and managerial perspectives in Kazakhstan
items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in innovation activities, yet firm-level evidence on variation across innovation stages and organizational conditions remains limited in emerging economies such as Kazakhstan. This study examines AI use among surveyed firms in Kazakhstan, focusing on stage-specific influence, organizational correlates, barriers, reported effects, and managerial perceptions. A cross-sectional voluntary survey yielded a non-probability sample of 93 firms; data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, exploratory bivariate analysis, multinomial logistic regression, and descriptive review of open-ended recommendations. In the sample, 39.8% reported no AI use in innovation activities; 23.7% used AI frequently or always. Idea generation was rated higher than idea testing and selection (r = .398), although concordance in stage rankings was weak (Kendall’s W = .077). The reported AI-related resource-category count was associated with both occasional (RRR = 6.98) and frequent AI use (RRR = 7.10) relative to no reported AI use in innovation activities. At the same time, firm size and age were not significant. Skills shortages, financial constraints, regulatory uncertainty, and ethical concerns were the leading barriers. Among firms reporting AI use in innovation activities, the most frequently reported effects were greater innovation-process efficiency (46.4%) and improved understanding of industry opportunities and trends (30.4%). items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Legal Research and Judicial Decision Support: Opportunities, Risks, and Accountability
items.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in legal research and judicial decision support. It examines the key technologies currently in use, the tangible benefits they offer (such as efficiency, cost reduction, and improved access to justice), and the critical risks that have emerged in practice (including algorithmic bias, opacity, automation bias, and confidentiality concerns). Furthermore, the paper proposes institutional governance measures and responsible workflows to ensure that AI innovation remains aligned with the core principles of the rule of law, including competence, candor, fairness, and reasoned decision-making. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Software Engineering: From Code Generation to Reasoning
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping software engineering in recent years. This transformation has moved beyond early code generation and completion tools toward systems capable of participating in requirements analysis, design, testing, debugging, documentation, and solving complex software problems. The aim of this review paper is to examine the evolving role of AI in software engineering, with a particular focus on the transition from code generation tools to reasoning-based infrastructures. In this study, relevant research and studies on the application of Large Language Models (LLMs), code generation tools, and intelligent systems across different phases of the software development lifecycle are reviewed and categorized. The distinction between automatic code generation and capabilities such as problem analysis, planning, multi-step reasoning, and solution evaluation is also discussed. Findings from the reviewed literature indicate that AI can evolve from an auxiliary tool for generating code fragments into an effective factor in supporting more complex software engineering processes. However, issues such as output correctness, reasoning errors, code security, dependence on training data, trustworthiness, and the necessity of human oversight remain significant challenges in this field. Finally, the paper emphasizes the need to move from a purely "code generation" perspective toward a more comprehensive approach based on human–AI collaboration in software engineering processes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence tools for developing research and academic writing skills among graduate students: An action research study
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed higher education by providing tools that support research and academic writing. This action research study examined changes in graduate students' research and academic writing outcomes following a structured six-week instructional intervention integrating Perplexity AI and Jenni AI. Seventeen graduate students participated in workshops on the effective and ethical use of both tools. Data were collected using pre- and post-intervention questionnaires and an analytical rubric evaluating students' research papers. The mean rubric score increased from 62.51 (SD = 9.80) to 86.47 (SD = 6.59) out of 100, t (16) = 8.26, p < .001, 95% CI [17.81, 30.10], Cohen's dz = 2.00. The overall questionnaire mean increased from 3.17 (SD = 0.56) to 4.42 (SD = 0.51) on a five-point Likert scale, t (16) = 7.99, p < .001, 95% CI [0.92, 1.59], Cohen's dz = 1.94. Participation in the structured AI-supported intervention was associated with substantial improvements in research-paper performance and self-reported research, writing, and AI-related outcomes. The findings also underscore the importance of ethical use, critical evaluation, and human oversight. Given the small single-group design, the results should be interpreted as evidence of pre–post change rather than proof of a causal effect attributable to either AI tool.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted cytology improves diagnostic consistency and accuracy in cervical cancer screening: A multicenter crossover study
items.abstract: Objectives: The effective prevention and control of cervical cancer (CC) depend on high-quality screening. However, traditional cytology interpretation faces challenges such as strong subjectivity, significant inter-observer variability, and a shortage of cytopathologists in primary care settings. The distribution of high-quality medical resources in China is highly uneven between urban and rural areas. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cytology offers a new approach to enhance screening efficacy. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a deep learning-based AI-assisted cytology system in a multicenter clinical environment in China, comparing its utility as a standalone tool and in a collaborative model with cytopathologists. Materials and Methods: This was a multicenter, crossover study enrolling a total of 769 outpatient liquid-based cytology samples obtained from three participating hospitals. Using a crossover design, two junior-to-mid-level cytopathologists from primary hospitals performed independent diagnoses and AI-assisted diagnoses (following an AI preliminary screening combined with cytopathologist verification), which were compared with AI-alone diagnoses. Using an expert cytology panel diagnosis as the cytological reference standard, sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), overall accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) negative predictive value, and false-positive rates/false-negative rates and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated and compared for each modality at the atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US+), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL+), and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+) thresholds. Results: The study found that the independent diagnostic Se of the primary cytopathologists was insufficient (LSIL+: 46.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.359–0.564)–50.6% (95% CI: 0.403–0.608); HSIL+: 36.6% (95% CI: 0.236–0.519)–46.3% (95% CI: 0.321–0.613), indicating a high risk of missed diagnoses. AI-alone diagnosis showed high Se (ASC-US+: 92.9% [95% CI: 0.877–0.960]) but a relatively lower PPV (72.0% [95% CI: 0.654–0.778]). AI-assisted diagnostic model achieved a favorable balance. Across all diagnostic thresholds, the AI-assisted modality significantly outperformed cytopathologist-alone diagnosis. At the ASC-US+ threshold, AI-alone Se was 92.9% (95% CI: 0.877–0.960) with a Sp of 90.9% (95% CI: 0.883–0.929), whereas the sensitivities of the two primary cytopathologists alone were 68.4% (95% CI: 0.607–0.752) and 81.3% (95% CI: 0.744–0.866), respectively. With AI assistance, primary cytopathologist Se increased to 92.3% (95% CI: 0.870–0.955)–94.2% (95% CI: 0.893–0.969), and Sp reached 94.6% (95% CI: 0.925–0.961)–96.9% (95% CI: 0.952–0.980). At the LSIL+ and HSIL+ thresholds, where cytopathologist-alone sensitivities were low (LSIL+: 46.0% [95% CI: 0.359–0.564]–50.6% [95% CI: 0.403–0.608]; HSIL+: 36.6% [95% CI: 0.236–0.519]–46.3% [95% CI: 0.321–0.613]), AI assistance improved them to 80.5% (95% CI: 0.709–0.874) and 73.2% (95% CI: 0.581–0.843)–75.6% (95% CI: 0.607–0.862), respectively, with Sp exceeding 97.0% in both cases. The AI-assisted diagnostic model is an effective strategy for achieving standardized, high-quality CC screening, particularly for promoting homogeneous services in regions with uneven healthcare resources.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, emotional well-being, and difficult dialogues in school settings
items.abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. In particular, so-called empathic conversational agents (Ortega-Ochoa et al., 2024) are artificial entities designed to elicit empathic responses from users (Hall & Woods, 2006) and to generate highly personalized simulated environments by modulating content, feedback, and task difficulty according to identified emotional factors. Such artificial conversations enable learners to engage in adaptive learning experiences in which their emotional state becomes an active variable in the regulation of the educational pathway. items.title: As effective as the teacher, but less motivating: a randomized controlled comparison of AI-generated and teacher feedback on students’ writing performance and intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

items.title: Aspectos éticos de la inteligencia artificial en las instituciones de educación superior
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence is generating rapid transformations in society and, particularly, in higher education institutions. Its incorporation offers significant opportunities for teaching and learning processes, but it also raises challenges related to academic integrity, privacy, bias, authorship, equity, plagiarism, and the generation of false information. This reflective essay aims to analyze the main ethical aspects associated with the use of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions and to highlight the responsibilities of the different actors within the educational community. Methodologically, the study adopted a qualitative, documentary, and reflective approach based on the critical analysis of recent scientific literature and documents from international organizations addressing ethics and the use of artificial intelligence in educational contexts. The analysis highlights the need to establish clear institutional policies, regulations, and guidelines that promote the ethical, transparent, and responsible use of these technologies. It is concluded that higher education institutions play a fundamental role in regulating their use, educating students and faculty, and promoting continuous ethical reflection to ensure that technological innovation is aligned with academic integrity, the protection of rights, and human responsibility.

items.title: Asymmetric Dependency and the Algorithmic Figuration
items.abstract: This article argues that AI-governed systems, and large language models in particular, introduce a novel dynamic into contemporary figurations: one of asymmetric dependency, in which people are materially, and increasingly affectively, dependent upon systems that are not, in turn, affectively dependent upon them. This condition attenuates the affectively reciprocal interdependency on which psychogenetic processes depend in Norbert Elias’s account of the civilising process and gives rise to what we distinguish as behavioural civilising: the shaping of observable conduct through monitored compliance rather than through the internalisation of restraint. Because such systems simulate human exchange whilst stripping it of its negative social consequences, they simultaneously suspend the shame functions through which figurational pressure is ordinarily converted into self-restraint and so exert decivilising pressures within the same figuration. Extended engagement with conversational AI also introduces generative reflection: a mode of exchange in which thought is elaborated and transformed rather than merely returned. We thereby extend the Eliasian framework whilst specifying the conditions under which psychogenetic processes are disrupted and transformed.

items.title: Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Education: The Contribution of Cognitive and Emotional Variables
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational contexts is profoundly transforming teaching and learning processes, creating new opportunities for personalized instruction while simultaneously raising pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges (Chen et al., 2020; ZawackiRichter et al., 2019). While traditional technology acceptance models have primarily emphasized the role of digital competencies and perceived usefulness (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003), more recent studies suggest that AI adoption is also shaped by emotional factors, including anxiety, distrust, fears of professional replacement, and concerns about the quality of the educational relationship (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Liu & Liu, 2025). Within this framework, the present study investigates the combined contribution of cognitive and emotional factors to the development of attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence, assuming that AI acceptance is a multidimensional process in which knowledge, competencies, and emotional experiences interact dynamically. items.title: Audit transformation in the era of artificial intelligence: an integrative literature review of AI’s impact on audit quality, professional skepticism, and auditor competence
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the external audit, focusing on three linked outcomes: audit quality, auditors' professional skepticism, and the competences auditors need. Design/methodology/approach – An integrative literature review of 18 peer-reviewed studies in accounting, auditing and information systems published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by recent standard-setting documents from the IAASB and the PCAOB. Studies are coded by AI application, audit phase, research method and outcome, and synthesised thematically. Findings – AI extends audit coverage from samples to full populations and improves anomaly detection, fraud prediction, the evaluation of estimates and the efficiency of routine procedures. Archival evidence links AI investment by audit firms to fewer restatements, lower fees and more accurate going-concern and internal control opinions. However, the benefits depend on the human–machine relationship: auditors may discount AI evidence (algorithm aversion) or accept it without sufficient challenge (automation bias), and both can impair judgment. Model opacity, data quality, accountability and limited guidance in auditing standards remain unresolved risks, although standard setters have begun to respond. Research limitations – The review is integrative rather than systematic, covers English-language studies only and relies mainly on evidence from the United States, Europe and large audit firms. Evidence on generative AI in auditing is still at an early stage. Implications – Audit firms should treat AI output as evidence to be evaluated, design workflows that prompt challenge and protect the development of junior staff. Standard setters should clarify how much assurance AI-based procedures provide, and educators should combine data analytics with judgment training. Originality – The review integrates technical, behavioural and institutional strands into a single framework in which AI is proposed to affect audit quality mainly through calibrated professional skepticism and auditor competence. It derives five testable propositions and a research agenda relevant to both developed and emerging audit markets.

items.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

items.title: Autonomous Collaborative Robotics in Drone Swarms: Advanced Control Strategies for Complex Environments
items.abstract: Drones that can fly around on their own in groups are really good at watching things, helping with disasters, and doing work in factories. They have a hard time working together, scaling up, and changing what they do when things get complicated. When one person or computer is in charge of all the drones, it takes too long to make decisions. When the drones make their decisions, they have a hard time not running into each other and saving energy. So, we made a way for drones to work together using artificial intelligence. This way uses various kinds of learning and lets the drones make their own decisions. We tried this way with computers, and it worked really well. The drones got better at working, did things faster, finished tasks, and did not run into each other as much, even when there were a lot of things in their way.

items.title: Becoming creative cyborgs: What role(s) for GenAI in the creative writing classroom?
items.abstract: This article reports on my action research study exploring the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing pedagogy at higher education level. Over twelve months, I conducted six pedagogical experiments across three London institutions, engaging fifty-two students in exploring AI’s functional dimensions: as ideation catalyst, collaborative tool, scaffolding mechanism, editorial assistant, research facilitator and assessment instrument. Using a critical realist framework, I examine what emerged from this systematic investigation: GenAI demonstrates clear affordances in particular contexts (research, translation, ideation generation) but significant limitations in others (editorial feedback, assessment, true creative collaboration). Students across all cohorts showed sophisticated critical awareness of AI’s training processes and ethical implications, and most remained cautious about deploying AI as a creative tool. The article argues that engaging with GenAI’s weaknesses might be its greatest pedagogical strength.

items.title: Between algorithm and agency: designing inclusion with universal design for learning in the age of generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence in education raises a question that goes beyond efficiency: can AI support inclusive design without weakening teacher agency? This study examines that tension through Universal Design for Learning (UDL), understood not as a checklist of accommodations but as a framework for anticipating learner variability and removing barriers from the outset. The recent UDL 3.0 Guidelines further emphasise affect, identity, belonging and participation, making inclusive design inseparable from the relational dimension of teaching (CAST, 2024). The study introduces the construct of Digital Affective Literacy, defined as the capacity to preserve inclusive and relational intentionality while working with generative systems. This competence involves recognising the persuasive fluency of AI outputs, resisting uncritical delegation and transforming technological support into an opportunity for reflection. The construct is grounded in the relationship between emotion and cognition (Immordino-Yang & Damasio, 2007), in the risk of cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016), and in the Vygotskian distinction between tools that execute a task and mediators that reorganise thought (Vygotsky, 1978). items.title: Between Algorithm and Relationship: The Perceptions of Future Support Teachers on Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This study explores the attitudes of a sample of approximately 1,000 prospective support teachers towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) using the GAAIS scale. Although participants accept AI as an operational scaffolding tool, they strongly reject algorithmic delegation in professional decisions. Statistical uncertainty about didactic personalization highlights a profound awareness: true inclusion requires human relational care. The contemporary educational horizon is strongly impacted by advanced algorithmic systems, moving towards what Floridi (2025) defines as the onlife condition: an integrated ecosystem in which the boundaries between physical and digital dissolve. Within this framework, teachers face a dual pressure: on the one hand, the technocratic push towards automation, on the other the "Frankenstein complex", understood as an ancestral fear of a technological dehumanization and a marginalization of their role (Lim & Kim, 2024). This tension is particularly evident in special teaching, which is strongly focused on empathy. items.title: Between simulated empathy and embodied care: a comparative review of the affective, relation and pedagogical dimensions in ai-mediated education
items.abstract: The essay is part of the growing body of research on artificial intelligence in educational setting, focusing on the transformation of the emotional and relational aspect of generative and conversational system. Starting from the research question regarding how the recent educational literature conceptualizes, discusses and problematizes the emotional support mediated by artificial intelligence and its relationship between embodied care and human educational relationships, the study adopts a comparative review approach to analyse the different ways in which these dimensions are defined, articulated, and problematized. The analysis examines scientific publications released between 2022 and 2026, a timeframe that corresponds to the most intense period of dissemination and accessibility of artificial intelligence systems, capable of simulating dialogical interaction, emotional support, affective personalization in the educational context. Through a strict and transparent selection process conducted on major international databases, in particular Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO, the study constructs a heterogeneous corpus of empirical studies, theoretical contributions and reviews that share a focus on the socio-emotional dimension of education mediated by artificial intelligence. items.title: Between Technical Efficiency and Affective Resistance: Evidence for an Ethical Integration of AI in Teacher Training
items.abstract: The evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reconfiguring educational systems, reshaping the tenets of knowledge and the relational dynamics of instructional practice. Within this transition, computational AI's evolution reconfigures educational systems, altering classroom ecology, dismantling vertical knowledge transmission, and shifting assessment toward higher-order skills (Luckin, 2018; Selwyn, 2019). Adopting a Critical AI Literacy framework (Veldhuis et al., 2025), this study emphasizes understanding algorithmic agency, ethical impacts, and algorithmic justice. Critical oversight operations rest on the Human-in-Command principle (Floridi, 2022), asserting assessment as a human prerogative rooted in a student's biography. This fosters an "augmented intelligence" where routine-free time enhances educational relationships, mitigating cognitive passivity from chatbots (Andler, 2024). Ultimately, Digital Affective Literacy empowers teachers as pedagogical directors of care (Pellerey, 2024). The study adopted a convergent parallel mixed methods design to analyse teachers' perceptions and self-efficacy levels regarding AI. items.title: Beyond comprehension
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in educational contexts has transformed how students encounter academic content, yet a fundamental question remains underexamined: Do English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners possess the critical literacy competencies needed to evaluate AI-generated texts? This study investigated whether students in Morocco’s Classes Préparatoires aux Grandes Écoles (CPGE)—one of the nation’s most academically selective post-secondary programs—demonstrate readiness for AI-era literacy demands. We developed a diagnostic assessment instrument, the Critical Reading Diagnostic Assessment (CRDA), designed to mirror common characteristics of AI-generated academic content: a confident, authoritative tone, a logical structure with subtle gaps, claims requiring verification, and culturally embedded assumptions. Thirty first-year CPGE students (M age = 18.6 years) evaluated argumentative passages across five critical dimensions: argument identification, evidence evaluation, assumption recognition, multi-source synthesis, and source criticism. Metacognitive self-assessment data were also collected. Results revealed systematic evaluation failures across all dimensions, with mean accuracy rates of only 18–39% and large effect sizes confirming substantial deficits (d = 1.11–2.25). Metacognitive analysis showed that students overestimated their abilities by 11–38 percentage points across all dimensions, indicating profound self-assessment inaccuracies.

items.title: Beyond self-report: evaluating authentic ai literacy in a continuing education context
items.abstract: Generative AI tools have moved rapidly into professional and organizational practice, outpacing individuals' capacity to use them well. Fluent, superficially convincing outputs foster automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automated systems and miss the errors they introduce (Goddard et al., 2012); field-experimental evidence shows AI assistance boosts performance within its current capability while just as reliably degrading it outside that boundary, a limit users cannot detect from fluency alone (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023; Fernandes et al., 2026). This motivates closer scrutiny of how AI literacy is measured. Most existing instruments rely entirely on self-report, including for the cognitive dimension (Ng et al., 2024), and show weak correlations with independently developed objective performance tests (Koch et al., 2024), with self-assessment errors that are not uniformly directional (Zhang et al., 2026). items.title: Beyond the maimed teacher: human-environment-technology triangulations for a new ontology of care and social productivity
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence into educational ecosystems does not merely constitute an instrumental addition; rather, it portends an ontological transformation that reconfigures contemporary regimes of truth, epistemic validation criteria, and processes of subjectification (Paparella, Mancarella, 2025). The core issue extends beyond evaluating whether algorithmic tools are beneficial or detrimental; instead, it demands an understanding of the structural conditions under which education can still authentically occur when the production of knowledge is structurally outsourced to predictive and automated systems. Within this conceptual landscape, the paradigm of the algorithmic self comes to the fore: an inflection of personal identity that is continuously co-constituted and reconfigured within a perpetual relational dialogue with digital technologies. Governed by the underlying logics of recommendation, profiling, and automated personalization, the algorithmic self is exposed to a progressive semantic impoverishment. items.title: Big Data Governance Framework for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence Decision Systems
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision systems has increased organizational dependence on large-scale data, making big data governance a critical requirement for ensuring reliable and responsible decision-making. Although AI systems are often evaluated based on predictive accuracy and computational performance, their trustworthiness is strongly influenced by the quality, security, privacy, traceability, and fairness of the data used throughout the AI lifecycle. This study aims to develop a Big Data Governance Framework for Trustworthy AI Decision Systems by integrating key governance dimensions with trustworthy AI requirements. A qualitative conceptual framework development approach was employed, supported by structured literature review, thematic synthesis, and design science research principles. Relevant literature on big data governance, trustworthy AI, data quality, privacy, security, explainability, accountability, fairness, and AI decision systems was reviewed to identify recurring concepts and research gaps. The results show that trustworthy AI decision systems require seven core governance dimensions: data quality governance, security and privacy governance, metadata and data lineage, bias and fairness control, explainability support, accountability mechanisms, and continuous monitoring. These dimensions strengthen trustworthy AI capabilities, including reliability, transparency, explainability, fairness, privacy preservation, security, robustness, and auditability. The proposed framework demonstrates that trustworthy AI is not only determined by algorithmic performance but also by strong data governance across the AI lifecycle. This study concludes that effective big data governance can improve decision accuracy, traceability, accountability, risk reduction, and stakeholder trust in AI-based decision systems.
