items.title: Brief, Handoff, Backbrief, Forecast, Review: A Communication Cycle for Safer Trauma and Surgical Intensive Care Unit Transitions
items.abstract: Safety in trauma and surgical critical care is inseparable from the reliability of communication at transitions of care. Handoffs are recurrent, high-risk moments in which teams transfer not only information but responsibility, prioritization, uncertainty, and contingency planning; failures at these points propagate into omissions, delayed escalation, and preventable harm to patients and strain on the workforce. Structured handoff tools improve completeness and clarity but inconsistently change hard clinical endpoints, and tools alone do not create the culture of safety on which high-reliability organizations (HROs) depend. This narrative review synthesizes civilian handoff research, human-factors and HRO theory, situation-awareness, psychological safety, trauma video review, and military medical lessons-learned into a single implementable framework for safer trauma and surgical intensive care unit (SICU) transitions. We propose a 5-stage communication cycle: (1) teams Brief before transfer to establish roles, a shared mental model, and anticipate threats; (2) Handoff using a structured tool matched to the transition; (3) Backbrief so the receiver synthesizes high-risk items and ownership; (4) Threat Forecast to state explicitly what may deteriorate and what triggers escalation; and (5) Post-hoc Review to convert selected transitions into learning. The stages map onto HRO hallmarks and depend on psychological safety, deference to expertise, and the inclusion of nurses and other frontline staff whose voices and well-being are integral to safe transitions. Because rare clinical endpoints are difficult to attribute, we offer a layered measurement framework spanning process, team-behavior, documentation, clinical, and workforce-culture measures. Reframing the handoff from a single script into a repeatable, high-reliability communication cycle offers trauma and SICU teams a scalable, adaptable strategy for enhancing safer health care systems.

items.title: Building peace in the digital age: towards an ontology of care and human relations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming how individuals communicate, learn, and build relationships. In education, its impact extends beyond technology, reshaping the construction of meaning and the experience of encounters with others. The pedagogical question, therefore, concerns not only what artificial intelligence is capable of doing but also what risks being redefined when relationships are interpreted according to the criteria of efficiency, immediacy, and functionality (Panciroli & Rivoltella, 2023). Accordingly, although generative systems are now capable of simulating forms of dialogue, listening, and apparently empathic support, it becomes essential to distinguish the simulation of relationships from genuine relational experience. The production of coherent and personalized responses does not, in fact, entail responsibility, reciprocity, vulnerability, or participation in a shared history. It is precisely this distinction that makes care an indispensable interpretative category for understanding the meaning of contemporary education. items.title: Can care be simulated? teachers' judgments of educational messages in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering educational practice as a tool for producing texts, designing materials and supporting instructional decisions. Its presence, though, does not concern only technical efficiency. It also affects the way educational language is perceived, especially when a message appears empathic, reassuring and pedagogically appropriate. The question addressed in this study is not whether AI can write correct educational responses, but whether such responses are recognized as expressions of care when their authorship is uncertain or attributed to either a teacher or an artificial system. Care is understood here not as emotional tone alone, but as a pedagogical relation grounded in attention, responsibility and situated judgment (Noddings, 2005). The study adopts an exploratory mixed-methods design with a quantitatively driven structure and an integrated qualitative component. An anonymous online questionnaire was administered to 807 participants enrolled in teacher qualification pathways at Link Campus University. items.title: Ceramic Design and the Role of Generative AI: A Practice-Based Exploration
items.abstract: Background: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into creative practice raises new questions for craft-based disciplines such as ceramic design, where digital ideation must ultimately be translated into physical, material form. Objectives: This study explores (RQ1) where and why the alignment of AI-generated concept imagery with hand-built ceramic outcomes fails; (RQ2) how prompt-based iteration with a general-purpose text-to-image model supports or hinders the progressive refinement of a single design; and (RQ3) what forms of human knowledge and intervention are necessary to translate AI-generated concepts into producible ceramic objects. Methods: Using a qualitative, practice-based methodology, the researcher employed a text-to-image generative AI tool (ChatGPT 4 Plus + DALL·E 3) to generate design concepts for three ceramic objects—a children’s plate, a house number plaque, and a wall panel—which were subsequently produced by hand in collaboration with a professional ceramic instructor. Results: In the hands of a designer with limited ceramic experience, production difficulties clustered where the AI image encoded constraints that were invisible to the prompt—contour line weight, color separation in small recesses, lettering, scale and modular tolerance. AI-generated alternatives were frequently visually compelling yet materially infeasible, and the tool could not support incremental refinement of a single design across prompts. Whether these failures reflect properties of the AI output or the maker’s skill ceiling cannot be fully separated in a single-operator study; what follows is therefore a provisional, criteria-stated attribution, in which each breakdown is assigned to its most plausible source and the residual uncertainty is flagged. Conclusion: Generative AI functioned as a co-creative ideation partner rather than an autonomous designer; the negotiation between AI-proposed imagery and material reality was carried out by the human maker, drawing on codified technical knowledge (firing, shrinkage, dimensions) as well as tacit, embodied skill (brushwork, contouring, judging what will “work in clay”).

items.title: ChatGPT and student engagement in L2 writing: a systematic review towards a ChatGPT-enabled smart learning environment framework
items.abstract: ChatGPT has become a part of the second language (L2) writing process as learners brainstorm ideas, seek feedback, and revise their texts. However, its pedagogical value depends on whether these interactions sustain behavioural, cognitive, and affective student engagement or contribute to disengagement. This systematic review synthesises research on ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing in the context of higher education concerning student engagement, examining patterns in research methods, theoretical perspectives, thematic findings, and future directions. The findings indicate that ChatGPT may both support and constrain student engagement, depending on learner characteristics, task design, feedback quality, and teacher guidance. The included studies highlighted that behaviourally, learners participated in planning and revision, but some relied heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) generated suggestions. Cognitively, ChatGPT prompted feedback evaluation and reflection, while inaccurate responses and cognitive offloading could limit deeper engagement. Affectively, learners reported motivation and reduced writing anxiety alongside frustration and a lack of interpersonal support. To organise the factors associated with both engagement and disengagement, the review proposes the preliminary ChatGPT-Enabled Smart Learning Environment (CESLE) framework which integrates engagement and disengagement factors and advances the concept of Ethical Human–AI Synergy through algorithmic stewardship, ethical collaborative intelligence, and an AI + teacher approach. The framework offers a context-sensitive foundation for supporting learner agency, responsible AI use, and sustained engagement in ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing. Thus, the review underscores the need for teacher-guided integration of AI that supports learners’ critical judgement and authorial voice.

items.title: Cognitive Effort Displacement in AI-Assisted Learning: Effects on Student Engagement and Knowledge Retention on TVET
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming teaching and learning in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) by providing personalized instructional support and improving access to learning resources. However, growing reliance on AI tools may reduce learners’ cognitive effort, leading to cognitive displacement with potential implication for student engagement and knowledge retention. This study investigated the extent of AI tool usage, the level of cognitive effort displacement, and the relationships among AI tool usage, cognitive effort displacement, student engagement, and knowledge retention among TVET students in Abia State, Nigeria. A descriptive correlational survey design was adopted. The study population comprised 2,400 TVET students, from which a sample of 343 respondents was selected using multistage sampling techniques. Data were collected using the Cognitive Effort Displacement, Engagement, and Retention Questionnaire (CEDERQ) (α = 0.85). Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, while Pearson product-moment correlation was employed to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed a high level of AI tool usage (x̄ = 3.47), a moderate to high level of cognitive effort displacement (x̄ = 3.26), and a high level of student engagement and knowledge retention (x̄ = 3.32). AI tool usage showed a significant positive relationship with cognitive effort displacement (r = 0.612, p < 0.05), whereas cognitive effort displacement had significant negative relationships with student engagement (r = –0.478, p < 0.05) and knowledge retention (r = –0.563, p < 0.05). The study concludes that while AI-assisted learning enhances instructional support in TVET, excessive dependence on AI may undermine active cognitive engagement and long-term knowledge retention. The study recommends pedagogical approaches that balance AI support with independent problem-solving and reflective learning.

items.title: Conceptual Framework for AI Enabled Learning and Sustainable Organizational Development
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to transform organizational learning and strengthen sustainable development. However, existing research often examines AI capability, organizational learning, digital innovation strategy, and sustainability separately. This study aims to develop an integrated conceptual framework explaining how AI-enabled organizational learning may contribute to sustainable organizational development. An integrative literature review was conducted using structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by citation tracking through Google Scholar. Thirty-one scholarly sources were synthesized according to their theoretical constructs, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis. The framework integrates the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capability Theory, Technology-Organization-Environment framework, and technology acceptance theories. The study proposes an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Learning Ecosystem (AILE) framework comprising four direct propositions linking AI Capability, AI-Enabled Learning Ecosystem, Digital Innovation Strategy, and Sustainable Organizational Development. Two additional propositions identify employee engagement and technology acceptance, alongside resource efficiency and AI governance, as moderating conditions. The framework also introduces organizational sustainability indicators, a resource cost-benefit assessment, and a four-stage implementation roadmap. The proposed framework offers a theoretical foundation for examining how AI-supported learning can contribute to organizational resilience, workforce development, and responsible digital innovation. Its potential relevance extends to SDGs 4, 8, and 9. As the framework remains conceptual, longitudinal and multilevel empirical studies are required to validate the proposed relationships and assess their practical effectiveness.

items.title: Dentists’ acceptance of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support for oral potentially malignant disorder detection: a structural equation modeling study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) may support early detection and clinical decision-making of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), but clinical implementation depends on dentists’ acceptance of AI-assisted clinical decision support. This study aimed to identify structural associations of AI acceptance among dentists using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 500 dentists. Construct validity and reliability were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypothesized associations were evaluated using structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation analysis. The extended TAM showed generally satisfactory measurement properties and good overall model fit. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention (β = 0.550), followed by AI-assisted clinical decision reliance (β = 0.220), perceived usefulness (β = 0.180), trust (β = 0.140), and perceived ease of use (β = 0.120). Significant indirect effects operated through attitude toward AI. The model explained 67.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Dentists reported favorable behavioral intention toward AI-assisted decision support for OPMD detection. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention. The findings are consistent with the extended TAM. Successful implementation will require explainable systems, clinician education, trust-building, and effective workflow integration. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations translate into actual clinical adoption. Understanding factors associated with dentists’ acceptance of AI may support the responsible integration of AI-assisted decision support into oral cancer screening pathways.

items.title: Design and preliminary validation of an AI enhanced game based learning environment for computational thinking in upper secondary education
items.abstract: Abstract Integrating generative artificial intelligence within game-based learning offers promising but still-maturing possibilities for computational thinking (CT) education. This developmental research study (Type I) reports the design and preliminary validation of an AI-enhanced game-based learning environment (AI-GBLE) for upper-secondary students. Grounded in constructivism, cognitive load theory, information processing theory, mental models theory, and game-based learning principles, the environment integrates six components on the Roblox platform—problem-based scenarios, learning resources, collaborative learning, a CT enhancement centre, scaffolding, and an AI coaching system combining a GPT-4-powered conversational non-player character with a rule-based adaptive difficulty engine—within an authentic Smart Greenhouse (Internet of Things) context. Following expert appraisal of content, instructional design, and media-technology quality by nine specialists, three per domain, 30 Grade 11 students in Thailand used the environment across eight 60-minute sessions over six weeks in a one-group pretest–posttest validation. Students showed pre–post gains of 3.07 points on the 20-point computational thinking test (Wilcoxon r = .86; Cohen’s d_av = 2.79) and 5.90 points on the 15-point achievement test (d_av = 3.23)—standardised effects inflated by ceiling compression—and reported strong immediate satisfaction across six acceptance dimensions (overall M = 4.64). Because the single-group design precludes causal attribution, these findings are interpreted as preliminary evidence—of feasibility, acceptability, and learning-related signals from a developed prototype—rather than as intervention effectiveness. The individual contributions of the AI coach, adaptive engine, and other components were not empirically established. The study contributes a theory-mapped design heuristic for AI-augmented game-based learning and identifies controlled comparisons, improved measurement, and mechanism-focused analyses as priorities for subsequent research.

items.title: Digital affective literacy and algorithmic mediation in the reconfiguration of educational relationships in higher education
items.abstract: Generative AI is reconfiguring educational relationships in higher education, entering university study in the passages where doubt, error, and the need for feedback emerge. The pedagogical question concerns the quality of the training experience when artificial responses become ordinary learning practices. The article presents digital affective literacy as a necessary skill for engaging with AI ethically, through critical judgment and responsibility, in continuity with developments in AI literacy and its affective domain (Cuomo, Biagini, & Ranieri, 2022; Pretorius & Cahusac de Caux, 2024). The theoretical framework integrates AI in education, AI literacy, ethics of educational technologies, pedagogical care, teacher reflexivity, flipped learning, and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The literature recognises the potential of AI for personalisation, accessibility, and study support, while recalling the role of educational mediation in preserving students' judgment (UNESCO, 2023). items.title: Digital Affective Literacy in Physical Education: A Comprehensive Review and an Exploratory Survey on Teachers' Perceptions of AI and Digital Technologies
items.abstract: Physical Education (PE) represents an emotionally rich learning environment where students experience continuous interactions, feedback loops, and embodied activities that strongly shape motivation, self-efficacy, and social participation. In recent years, this context has been increasingly influenced by digital technologies and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) systems. International evidence indicates that the combination of digital tools and social-emotional learning (SEL) pathways can significantly enhance students' outcomes in PE, supporting motivation, engagement, and inclusive participation (Saqinah et al., 2025). At the same time, a recent scoping review of 63 studies highlights that SEL development in PE remains theoretically fragmented and only partially aligned with the main pedagogical models adopted in the field (Dyson et al., 2021). This gap suggests the need for frameworks capable of integrating emotional, relational, and technological dimensions in a coherent and ethically grounded manner. items.title: Digital financial literacy and trust in hybrid AI advisory: Explaining perceived private wealth management capability among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging market
items.abstract: This study investigates how digital financial literacy, perceived transparency of artificial intelligence advisory services, investment and wealth knowledge, and cyber-risk self-protection shape Perceived Private Wealth Management Capability (PWMC) among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging-market context. PWMC is conceptualized as a self-assessed capability outcome rather than an objective indicator of wealth-management performance, portfolio returns, or private-banking status. Drawing on the financial capability framework, trust in automation theory, and protection motivation theory, the study develops a trust-to-capability model in which trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory and digital wealth management behavior serves as a key explanatory mechanism. A non-probability sample of 249 digitally engaged retail investors in Vietnam was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling in SmartPLS 4.1, with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. The results show that digital financial literacy is the strongest antecedent of trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory (β = 0.517, p < 0.001). At the same time, perceived advisory transparency also exerts a significant positive effect (β = 0.261, p < 0.001). Investment and wealth knowledge emerged as the strongest predictor of digital wealth management behavior (β = 0.348, p < 0.001). Trust, digital wealth management behavior, and investment and wealth knowledge each positively influence perceived private wealth management capability. Digital wealth management behavior partially mediates the effects of trust, investment, and wealth knowledge on perceived capability. Cyber-risk self-protection limited evidence of a boundary condition by strengthening the relationship between trust and digital wealth management behavior. However, the effect size is small and should be interpreted cautiously (β = 0.098, p = 0.038). The model explains 60.2% of the variance in digital wealth management behavior and 44.3% of the variance in perceived private wealth management capability. By moving beyond conventional explanations of robo-advisory adoption and technology acceptance, this study theorizes hybrid AI advisory as a calibrated trust environment in which retail investors’ perceived capability depends not only on whether they trust AI-supported advice but also on whether that trust translates into protective, enacted digital wealth management behavior. The findings should be interpreted in the context of digitally engaged retail investors. They should not be generalized to private banking clients, high-net-worth investors, objective portfolio performance, or verified wealth outcomes.

items.title: Digital Tools for Risk Assessment and Decision-Making in Business Operations
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper analyses how digital tools such as artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital twin technologies can enhance risk assessment and decision-making in business operations. Design/Methodology/Approach: The research studies the existing literature on digital transformation and risk management, drawing on 29 publications from 2020 to 2026 (27 journal articles published in the Scopus database and two book chapters). The publications are analysed using thematic synthesis based on three constructs: digital tools, risk assessment capability, and decision-making performance. Research Limitation: The study is based on existing literature, indicating the need for further research on the practical implementation of digital technologies in different business environments. Findings: The results suggest that introducing digital technologies into management systems speeds decision-making, improves risk management, and makes organisations more competitive. Digital technologies enable organisations to process large amounts of real-time data, detect potential risks, and support more informed, timely managerial decisions. Practical Implication: The findings show that digital tools can improve risk assessment procedures and support more effective managerial decision-making. Social Implication: More efficient decision-making and risk management contribute to greater organisational resilience in dynamic business environments. Originality/Value: The study addresses two gaps in the literature: insufficient analysis of technology combinations and the human factor. In its tool-to-capability framework, digital tools contribute to operational performance indirectly by affecting risk assessment and decision-making, an effect the synthesis links to governance and managerial competencies.

items.title: Domain Knowledge Plus AI Fluency: The New Nonnegotiable Competency for the Health Workforce in the AI Era
items.abstract: In the ongoing AI boom—now supercharged by large language models and generative AI tools—the rapid integration of AI into health care and public health has created an urgent need for professionals who combine deep domain expertise (clinical, epidemiological, ethical, and contextual expertise in health and public health) with AI fluency (the ability to understand, critically evaluate, use, and oversee AI systems effectively). Without domain guidance, AI risks producing biased, unsafe, or contextually irrelevant outputs that compromise patient safety and exacerbate disparities. Conversely, domain experts lacking AI fluency may underuse or misuse these technologies, missing opportunities to improve care quality, operational efficiency, and population health. A foundational understanding of the modern AI system stack—comprising energy, accelerators, infrastructure, models, and applications—empowers health professionals to make informed decisions on adoption, evaluation, governance, and ethical use without needing to code or build models themselves. This stack framework highlights critical interdependencies and health care–specific challenges, including regulatory compliance, data privacy, sustainability, and resource constraints, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This paper argues that cultivating domain-AI bilingualism is essential for safe, effective, and equitable AI integration worldwide. It outlines the 5-layer AI system stack applied to health care, key reasons for hybrid expertise, and a practical 4-step pathway: awakening (recognizing AI’s transformative role), intrepidity (courageously engaging foundational AI concepts), bilingualism (translating between clinical needs and AI capabilities), and visionary leadership (driving organizational and policy readiness). It outlines major barriers, targeted strategies, and recommendations for educators, institutions, and policymakers. By bridging domain knowledge with AI fluency, health professionals can direct—rather than be directed by—AI technologies, including emerging agentic systems, toward more precise, sustainable, and human-centered outcomes while mitigating risks. This hybrid capability represents a nonnegotiable competency for the health workforce for thriving in the post-2026 AI era.

items.title: Dynamic PGA: A Human-Centered Framework for Continuously Adaptive AI Experiences
items.abstract: Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) is a human-centered conceptual framework for continuously adaptive AI experiences. The framework explores how artificial intelligence might adapt not only to an individual's longer-range goals, interests, knowledge, and preferences, but also to meaningful changes that occur as an experience unfolds. The paper introduces a developing Dynamic A/B model: Dynamic A provides adaptive direction around the individual's goals and intended destination, while Dynamic B introduces state-aware responsiveness to the individual's immediate circumstances. Together, they express a central principle of the framework: A remembers the destination. B respects the human being who has to get there. Version 1.0 explores potential applications in education, experiential travel, professional environments, healthcare communication, and creative work, while emphasizing human agency, privacy, appropriate boundaries, and future research and validation.

items.title: Economic Sustainability as a Factor of Resilience of Economic Systems in the Crisis-Digital Paradigm of Sustainable Development Management
items.abstract: Purpose: To examine the relationship between economic sustainability, innovation, and sustainable development as key determinants of the resilience of modern economic systems and identify strategic approaches for strengthening resilience through digital transformation. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study employed a qualitative research design based on a systematic review of scientific literature, comparative analysis, and conceptual synthesis. The review covered 31 studies (2020–2026) retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, supplemented by Google Scholar, and identified the principal mechanisms that enhance the adaptability and long-term stability of economic systems. Research Limitation: The study is conceptual and based on secondary sources. Future research should validate the proposed framework using empirical evidence from different sectors. Findings: The results show that economic sustainability is closely linked to integrating technological and digital innovations into production and management processes. Structural adaptability, system integration, stakeholder participation, human capital development, and effective resource management were identified as key prerequisites for sustainable growth and resilience. items.title: Edukasi AI untuk Siswa Kelas VI Sekolah Dasar Negeri 26 Kota Bengkulu
items.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology makes it important for young learners to become familiar with the basic concepts of artificial intelligence (AI). Many elementary school students use AI-enabled applications in their daily lives, such as voice assistants and content recommendation systems, without necessarily understanding how these technologies work. This community service activity introduced basic AI concepts to 28 Grade VI students at State Elementary School 26, Bengkulu City, on 27 August 2026, through interactive lectures, educational games, question-and-answer sessions, and simple demonstrations. Descriptive observations of student participation during the activities indicated enthusiasm and engagement with examples of AI, its benefits, and its risks. No formal evaluation instrument, pre-test/post-test scores, or numerical outcome measurements were available; therefore, the extent of learning improvement cannot be quantified. The activity provides an initial model for introducing age-appropriate AI literacy in elementary schools.

items.title: Emerging Technologies and Assessment Innovation in European Online Higher Education
items.abstract: Digital assessment has become a strategic component of online higher education, supporting not only the certification of learning outcomes but also feedback processes, student monitoring and quality assurance (JISC, 2020). Recent technological developments have expanded the possibilities of assessment through Artificial Intelligence (AI), learning analytics and immersive technologies, which are increasingly associated with personalised feedback, adaptive assessment, data-informed decision making and authentic learning experiences (Holmes et al., 2023; Kamalov et al., 2023). While the educational potential of these technologies has been widely discussed, less attention has been devoted to their institutional formalisation. Technological innovation does not automatically translate into institutional adoption. Universities may experiment with innovative tools without integrating them into policies, governance structures, assessment strategies or quality assurance systems. For this reason, understanding how emerging technologies are represented within institutional documentation can provide valuable insights into the maturity of digital assessment ecosystems. items.title: Engagement of Older Adults with AI-Supported Healthcare Systems and the Risks of Age-Based Exclusion
items.abstract: This article argues that older adults’ engagement with healthcare systems supported by artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be explained solely by access to technology or individual levels of digital literacy. The central claim is that when older adults are unable to benefit fully from these systems, the problem is often framed as a personal failure to adapt, whereas the deeper issue is a form of sociotechnical exclusion produced at the intersection of data representation, design norms, limited explainability, inadequate institutional support, and age-based bias. To explore this issue, the article draws on a composite case involving an older woman who struggles to use an AI-supported chronic disease monitoring application. It first examines the opportunities associated with artificial intelligence in the care of older adults and the conceptual tensions surrounding these technologies. It then presents the composite case and analyses it through the lenses of digital exclusion, digital ageism, participatory design, care ethics, and nursing practice. The article concludes that the success of artificial intelligence in healthcare should be assessed not only in terms of accuracy, speed, and efficiency, but also in terms of its capacity to involve older adults in care processes in ways that are understandable, safe, fair, and dignified.

items.title: Estrategia pedagógica basada en inteligencia artificial generativa en el aprendizaje autodirigido de estudiantes de Enfermería
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to strengthen self-directed learning in nursing education when its integration is supported by a structured pedagogical design. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the E-PAGIA strategy, organized into planning, construction, self-monitoring, and interaction/transfer stages, on self-directed learning among nursing students. A quantitative, quasi-experimental, longitudinal study was conducted with 128 students, distributed between an experimental group and a control group, with 64 participants in each. The intervention lasted eight weeks. Self-directed learning was assessed using the Self-Directed Learning Instrument, considering both the overall score and its dimensions. The groups showed comparable baseline scores. Following the intervention, the experimental group increased its mean overall score from 65.00 to 82.35 points, whereas the control group increased from 65.75 to 69.46. Improvements in the experimental group were observed across all four dimensions and were particularly pronounced in learning motivation and planning and implementation. Analysis adjusted for baseline scores confirmed significant differences between groups and showed a large effect associated with the strategy. The findings indicate that E-PAGIA can foster self-directed learning when generative artificial intelligence is integrated as cognitive support within a pedagogical sequence that preserves students' intellectual responsibility, teacher mediation, and critical verification of information. The study concludes that E-PAGIA represents a relevant pedagogical innovation for nursing education.

items.title: Ethical Boundaries in Human-AI Collaborative Decision Systems: A Review
items.abstract: This review covers human–artificial intelligence collaboration in making decisions, observing how scholarship has moved from thinking of AI as a passive tool to considering it as an active actor in healthcare, management, and ethics. While AI systems provide for efficient data processing and pattern recognition, humans provide contextual understanding, ethical judgment, creativity, and accountability. Previous literature suggests that well-designed collaboration between humans and AI may outperform completely automated decision-making. However, several key challenges persist, like bias, lack of transparency, miscalibrated trust, poorly defined distribution of roles, and accountability gaps. To handle these concerns, human-centered design, explainability in AI, well-articulated guidelines on ethical consideration, and mechanisms that effectively introduce oversight remain at the core of literature. These approaches jointly try to ensure that human–AI decision-making systems are fair, accountable, and trustworthy in high-stakes and critical settings

items.title: Evolution of Financial AI: From Statistical Models to Agentic AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in finance has evolved from statistical learning and machine learning for structured prediction, through deep learning and foundation models for representation learning, language understanding, and reasoning, to retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-grounded reasoning and agentic AI for autonomous planning and execution. In this paper, we examine how researchers and practitioners can select and apply AI methods in finance. We first show that the major paradigms of financial AI address fundamentally different classes of problems, rather than forming a strict hierarchy of capability. We then review the current state of research on AI in finance and trace how these paradigms have reshaped financial data, financial tasks, decision support, and human-AI collaboration. Building on this, we propose practical guidelines for matching AI paradigms to task characteristics, and show that more advanced models, such as foundation models or autonomous agents, are not universally superior. We conclude by outlining open challenges for researchers and practitioners working toward reliable financial AI.
